records.name: Cell lineage, identity and state
records.tldr: A cell’s ancestry, its type and its current activity answer different questions. Similar activity does not prove that two cells share a recent ancestor.
records.summary: Lineage describes descent from earlier cells. A cell type or identity describes a differentiated family, while a state describes context-dependent features such as activation, stress or cycling. A genetic clone has shared ancestry and can be tracked through specified genomic features; an RNA cluster alone does not establish that ancestry. Stem cells can renew and generate descendants; progenitor potential is restricted by the biological context. Differentiation develops specialized properties without requiring every change of state to become a new lineage.

notes: Reference atlases classify measured features. Barcodes or other validated tracing information add ancestry evidence, with their own labeling and sampling limits. Weinreb and colleagues combined expressed barcodes and transcriptomes over time in hematopoiesis; sister-cell analyses exposed fate biases that a single RNA snapshot missed. This does not identify an individual tumor’s origin from its expression profile.

records.name: Epithelium, stroma and tissue compartments
records.tldr: Tissue contains different cell groups and supporting material. Knowing which compartment produced a signal helps explain what the result can mean.
records.summary: Epithelium forms linings, coverings and glands; an epithelial cell is not necessarily malignant. A basement membrane is extracellular supporting material beneath an epithelium, distinct from each cell’s lipid membrane. Stroma includes supporting cells, extracellular matrix and vascular structures, rather than only collagen or fibroblasts. Immune cells and other nonmalignant cells can contribute to a tumor specimen. The relevant compartments depend on the tissue and disease.

notes: Bulk RNA or protein measurements combine contributions from sampled cells. A stronger signal can reflect more cells of one type, changed expression within cells, or both. Spatial review and suitable cell markers help test attribution; a mixed-tissue result should not automatically be assigned to cancer cells. Normal and cancer breast atlases provide defined examples of this cellular diversity.

An epithelial marker helps identify a cell compartment; a positive lineage stain alone does not establish malignancy or invasion. Tissue architecture matters. For an epithelial carcinoma, assessing in-situ versus invasive disease includes microscopic review of the basement membrane and surrounding tissue. The SEER summary-stage manual retains site-specific exceptions; this boundary is not a universal staging rule for every cancer.

records.name: Organelles and cellular compartments
records.tldr: A cell has compartments with different jobs. A molecule inside one compartment may still be separated from the place where it needs to act.
records.summary: The nucleus houses most cellular DNA; mitochondria have their own genome and participate in energy metabolism and other processes. Ribosomes make polypeptide chains. The endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi process and sort selected membrane or secreted cargo, while lysosomes degrade delivered material in an acidic compartment. That itinerary is not the route of every protein. Cytosol is the fluid outside membrane-bound organelle interiors; cytoplasm includes cytosol and structures outside the nucleus. A vesicle lumen is not cytosol.

records.name: Alleles, zygosity and copy state
records.tldr: An allele is a sequence version at a genomic location. Which versions are present and how many DNA copies exist are separate questions.
records.summary: At a diploid location, heterozygous means that the two copies differ in the feature being considered; homozygous means they match. Hemizygous describes a single copy in the specified context. Tumor gains, losses and genome doubling can make a two-copy model inadequate. Loss of heterozygosity means loss of previously different allelic information; it can accompany a deletion or occur while total copy count remains unchanged. Total copy number alone cannot identify which allele was retained.

Purity, local copy state, subclonal mixtures and method affect it; it is not directly a cancer-cell percentage or a zygosity call. Phase asks whether specified variants share a DNA copy, a further question that a gene-name match does not answer.

records.name: Epigenetic marks and DNA methylation
records.tldr: Chemical features of DNA and its packaging can influence how genes are used. Their location and cellular context matter; a mark does not have one universal effect.
records.summary: DNA methylation changes a base’s chemical state without substituting the underlying sequence letter. Much human methylation analysis concerns 5-methylcytosine at CpG sites. Histone modifications affect DNA-associated proteins and are distinct from marks on DNA itself. Some regulatory states persist through division; epigenetic does not mean every mark is permanent or transmitted between generations. Promoter methylation can participate in reduced transcription, while patterns elsewhere need their own interpretation.

notes: Standard bisulfite analysis changes unmodified cytosine but reads both 5-methylcytosine and 5-hydroxymethylcytosine as C. Oxidative bisulfite methods separate those features through additional chemistry. Ordinary amplified DNA sequence does not preserve this direct chemical measurement.

A methylation signal in mixed tissue is not a percentage of cancer cells with a silenced gene. Cell mixture, genomic location, conversion controls and method resolution matter. Association with low RNA does not establish causation or treatment sensitivity.

records.name: Nonsense-mediated RNA decay
records.tldr: A cell can reduce some RNA messages when translation stops in an unexpected context. A predicted early stop does not guarantee that every message or protein disappears.
records.summary: Nonsense-mediated decay is RNA surveillance coupled to translation termination. Splicing can leave exon junction protein complexes near later joins in the message. Translation can remove junction-associated proteins; early termination while an appropriate complex remains downstream can help recruit decay machinery in one human route. Stop position, exon architecture, proximity to the start and other transcript features affect susceptibility. A common junction-distance shortcut is a hypothesis, not a universal clinical cutoff.

Test the relevant transcript or allele with controls for RNA quality and cell mixture. Protein identity, persistence and function need separate measurements: RNA decay is distinct from protein degradation.

records.name: V(D)J recombination and receptor assembly
records.tldr: Developing lymphocytes assemble receptor genes from selected DNA segments. Making a receptor is separate from showing what it recognizes or whether it produces a useful response.
records.summary: Variable, diversity and joining segments provide the V, D and J names. Antibody heavy and conventional T-cell-receptor beta chains use VDJ arrangements; antibody light and T-cell-receptor alpha chains use VJ. RAG1/RAG2 recognize recombination signals and initiate DNA cutting; classical non-homologous end-joining repair machinery processes and joins coding ends, adding sequence diversity. Purified-protein cutting experiments and RAG1-deficient mouse experiments established distinct mechanistic requirements. RAG proteins are not the general repair machinery for every DNA break.

Receptor sequence or clonality does not establish antigen specificity, tumor recognition or malignant diagnosis. RAG RNA/protein presence alone does not establish active recombination.

Off-target RAG rearrangement must be interpreted in its cellular and sequence context. In the 2014 ETV6-RUNX1 acute lymphoblastic leukemia study, the authors found breakpoint recombination-signal motifs, junctional additions and enrichment at active B-development promoters and enhancers; single-cell analysis supported continuing rearrangement in the examined leukemias. This is evidence from that disease context, not a demonstration that RAG expression in any sampled cell proves active cutting or the same mechanism.

Different rearrangement paths can produce the same receptor amino-acid sequence. Influenza-specific mouse TCR-beta analysis and a separate human naive/memory CD8 T-cell study support convergent recombination and receptor sharing. The human study sampled four individuals; neither study establishes an individual cancer response. A shared receptor sequence or an expanded sequence count alone does not establish unique recent ancestry, antigen specificity or tumor killing.

records.name: Protein structure, domains and model confidence
records.tldr: A protein’s sequence, folded regions and contacts describe different features. A confident prediction of one region does not establish the whole molecule’s arrangement or function.
records.summary: Primary structure describes sequence; secondary structure describes local arrangements; tertiary structure describes a chain’s organization; quaternary structure describes assembly between chains. These are levels of description, rather than four obligatory stages. A domain is a recognizable structural unit; a motif is a recurring sequence or structural pattern. An interface is a contact surface and can combine residues far apart in sequence. Intrinsically disordered regions can have normal functions without one stable isolated fold.

notes: Experimental structures reflect particular preparations and conditions, and may omit flexible regions. In AlphaFold2, pLDDT concerns local structural confidence, while predicted aligned error helps assess uncertainty in relative region placement. A confident domain cannot certify a proposed inter-domain pocket or contact. Neither score measures binding affinity, protein abundance, a variant’s functional effect or clinical benefit.

X-ray crystallography interprets diffraction from crystals; crystallization and flexible regions constrain what can be resolved. NMR uses signals and spatial restraints, often in solution, and can report an ensemble of compatible structures. Single-particle cryo-electron microscopy combines many projections of particles preserved in ice into a three-dimensional map. Each route requires preparation, experimental data and model interpretation. Check the method, local support, missing regions and validation of the actual structure; an atomic-looking model is not a direct photograph of every molecular state or proof of binding or function.

records.name: Binding affinity, occupancy and enzyme kinetics
records.tldr: Binding strength, the fraction of sites occupied and the speed of a reaction describe different things. Each measurement needs its experimental conditions.
records.summary: For a simple reversible binding equilibrium, Kd is the product of free partner concentrations divided by complex concentration; lower Kd means tighter binding under those conditions. For identical independent sites with one ligand and no competition, fractional occupancy is L / (Kd + L), where L is free ligand concentration. Half occupancy occurs at L = Kd in that model. Total added ligand need not equal free ligand. Affinity for one partner does not establish specificity against other partners.

notes: For a suitable Michaelis-Menten enzyme model, Km is the substrate concentration at half the maximum initial reaction rate. It depends on the catalytic mechanism and conditions and is not generally Kd. Turnover concerns reaction cycling, not binding strength.

IC50 is half inhibition of a specified assay response; EC50 describes half of a defined functional response change. Substrate/ATP concentrations, enzyme or receptor amount, timing and assay design affect these measures. A biochemical inhibition value, a cell-growth value and a clinical outcome are separate evidence.

records.name: Feedback, feedforward and signaling dynamics
records.tldr: A signal can change the circuit that produced it. Returning inhibition, returning reinforcement and a separate forward route can create different responses over time.
records.summary: Negative feedback returns a restraining effect to an upstream process; positive feedback reinforces it. These names describe direction, not clinical desirability. Feedforward sends an input through direct and indirect routes to an output without a returning connection. Connections, delays and cell state can produce transient, sustained or oscillating behavior. A positive loop does not always make an irreversible switch, and rebound need not require a new mutation.

O’Reilly and colleagues examined released feedback after mTOR inhibition in cancer models with patient-tumor pharmacodynamic observations. Neither study establishes universal tumor wiring or combination-treatment benefit.

Use time-resolved measurements and controlled perturbation of the proposed connection, with exposure and viability controls. Similar curves can arise from different circuits; a diagram or one late signal cannot identify the mechanism.

records.name: Receptor reserve and system-dependent response
records.tldr: A cell can sometimes reach its largest measured response without occupying every receptor. Receptor amount and downstream amplification help determine that response.
records.summary: Receptor reserve describes a system in which maximal functional response can be obtained before all available receptors are occupied. Occupancy and response can therefore have different concentration-response curves. Operational receptor models separate binding, receptor abundance or activation, and downstream transduction. An EC50 lower than a binding Kd is not on its own evidence of tighter binding. Changing receptor expression or amplification can alter apparent potency and the observed maximum of a partial agonist.

notes: Black and Leff developed an operational model; the later two-state model explicitly separates binding, activation and amplification and examines receptor-reserve data. These are quantitative pharmacology frameworks, not clinical dose-selection rules. Testing reserve requires functional and binding evidence or controlled changes in receptor availability with appropriate model checks.

records.name: Biased agonism and pathway-dependent receptor response
records.tldr: Two ligands at the same receptor can favor measured response pathways differently. That comparison depends on the reference ligand, assays and cellular system.
records.summary: Biased agonism compares the relative signaling behavior of ligands across specified outputs at the same receptor. Binding, intrinsic receptor activation, pathway amplification and baseline activity can contribute differently to observed curves. A potency difference between two assays does not by itself isolate ligand-specific bias. Preserve the reference ligand, endpoints, receptor expression, timing and model assumptions used to estimate it.

The constitutively active-mutant approach assumes that the mutation changes receptor-state equilibrium without changing ligand affinities and requires checking that assumption. These method studies do not establish clinical superiority of a biased ligand or validate every cellular assay.

records.name: Promoters, enhancers and transcription factors
records.tldr: Genes are regulated through DNA regions, binding proteins and cellular context. A bound regulator or accessible DNA region does not prove that a gene’s output changed.
records.summary: A promoter is a DNA region where transcription machinery assembles. Enhancers influence transcription through regulatory interactions, sometimes across a long linear distance brought together in three-dimensional space. Transcription factors recognize sequence features and participate in regulatory networks. Chromatin state and cellular partners affect access and function. Regulation also occurs through RNA processing and removal, translation, and protein modification or turnover.

notes: RNA measurements, chromatin accessibility, protein occupancy and reporter activity answer different questions. Binding or an open region alone does not establish regulation of a particular gene. Controlled perturbation can test a proposed causal connection, with controls for indirect effects and assay context.

records.name: Central dogma and molecular information flow
records.tldr: DNA copying, making RNA and making a protein are different processes. Following the route helps identify what each molecular test actually measured.
records.summary: Replication makes DNA from DNA. Transcription uses a DNA template to make RNA. Translation reads the coding sequence of a message in three-base codons to build a polypeptide; the transcript and reading frame matter. Functional noncoding RNAs do not need to become protein. Reverse transcription copies RNA into DNA in relevant viral and retrotransposon contexts. This information-flow map is not a guarantee that every DNA change produces a measured RNA or protein change.

notes: RNA processing, translation, folding, modification, localization and turnover can alter the path from a coding sequence to a functional product. DNA presence, RNA abundance, intact protein, location and activity require their own evidence. Neither a gene-level RNA count nor a sequence prediction establishes a fixed protein amount or clinical effect.

records.name: Cell membrane
records.tldr: The cell membrane forms a selective boundary. Binding at the surface, entering a vesicle and reaching the cell’s internal working fluid are different steps.
records.summary: A lipid bilayer and its proteins separate the cell from its surroundings. Permeability depends on size, charge and chemical properties, rather than a universal small-molecule versus antibody rule. Passive movement follows the relevant gradient; active transport uses energy directly or through a coupled gradient. Endocytosis encloses material in a membrane-bound compartment. Delivery to cytosol or another target compartment requires further steps. Cytosol is fluid outside organelle interiors; cytoplasm includes that fluid and structures outside the nucleus.

records.name: Cell cycle
records.tldr: Cells preparing to divide pass through regulated stages for growth, DNA copying and chromosome separation. Some cells remain functional while outside that cycle.
records.summary: G1 prepares the cell, S copies DNA, and G2 precedes the mitotic phase. Mitosis separates nuclear chromosomes; cytokinesis separates cytoplasm into daughter cells. G0 describes a noncycling state, which need not mean death or loss of function. Cyclins, CDKs and checkpoints regulate transitions, and their alteration can contribute to cancer without making every checkpoint absent or guaranteeing error-free division. Cell-cycle checkpoints and immune checkpoints describe different biological processes.

A Ki-67-positive fraction or snapshot phase distribution is not a division rate or a population doubling time. Time-resolved proliferation and cell-loss measurements answer further questions. CDK4/6 inhibitors and spindle-directed drugs affect different parts of the cycle.

records.name: Cell division
records.tldr: Cell division produces daughter cells for growth and renewal. Chemotherapy can disrupt this process and can also affect cells through mechanisms beyond division.
records.summary: DNA copying, chromosome segregation and cytokinesis are distinct steps; errors or unequal allocation can make daughters differ. Many cytotoxic drugs affect DNA or microtubules, with drug-specific dependence on cell-cycle state. Normal renewing tissues can also be affected. Division history cannot be read directly from a mutation count: damage, repair, selection and other processes contribute. Ki-67 staining and a mitotic count describe particular sampled properties, not a universal rate of cell production.

A lower cell count at one time can reflect slower division, cell loss or both; surviving cells may later resume growth. Colony-formation assays assess whether individual cells can produce descendants under the chosen culture conditions over a longer observation period. The result depends on the model and assay format. Neither a short growth assay nor colony formation alone establishes durable tumor control in a person.

records.name: Differentiation
records.tldr: Differentiation develops specialized cellular properties. In pathology, resemblance to a mature tissue can contribute to grading, whose meaning depends on the cancer.
records.summary: Differentiation concerns development of specialized cell features and functions. Stem or progenitor ancestry, current state and genetic clone are distinct questions. In cancer pathology, well or poorly differentiated describes resemblance to a mature tissue within the applicable classification; it is not a universal rule that one category grows at a particular speed. Tumor plasticity can change marker expression or lineage programs. A present-day expression cluster alone does not reconstruct the cell’s ancestry or prove a reversal of its developmental history.

records.name: Epithelial-mesenchymal transition & drug efflux
records.tldr: Epithelial cells can change a coordinated set of properties, sometimes entering intermediate states. The consequences depend on the cells and the experimental or clinical context.
records.summary: Epithelial-mesenchymal transition describes coordinated changes in cellular organization and programs, occurring in development, repair and disease. It is not a binary switch defined by one marker. Primary skin and mammary tumor studies identified intermediate epithelial/mesenchymal states with differing properties. Associations with migration, stem-like features, immune effects or drug resistance require context-specific evidence; they should not all be assigned automatically to every mesenchymal signal.

records.name: Germline vs somatic mutations
records.tldr: A DNA change can be inherited, newly constitutional or acquired in a cell lineage. A change found in a tumor is not automatically tumor-specific.
records.summary: Inherited germline variants came through an egg or sperm and are generally present across many tissues. A de novo constitutional variant need not have been inherited from a parent. Changes arising after fertilization can create mosaic distributions. Somatic variants occur in body-cell lineages, including normal tissues as well as cancers. Origin, distribution, harmfulness and transmissibility are separate questions; neither a variant class nor a large read fraction settles them.

records.name: DNA
records.tldr: DNA stores sequence information. Its packaging, copying and use as a template for RNA are different processes.
records.summary: DNA contains nucleotide chains with a sugar–phosphate backbone and the bases A, T, C and G. Complementary A–T and C–G pairing joins antiparallel strands. Nuclear chromosomes contain DNA associated with proteins as chromatin; nucleosomes organize DNA around histones. Mitochondria carry a separate genome. A gene is a functional region within DNA, rather than an entire chromosome. Replication copies DNA, while transcription produces RNA from a selected template. Packaging and gene presence do not establish active transcription or a functional protein.

Experimental work also shows that this signal is not an unambiguous count of double-strand breaks. A sequencing variant call, a lesion assay and a damage-response stain answer different questions; one is not a count of the others.

records.name: RNA
records.tldr: RNA is a family of molecules with several jobs. Messenger RNA provides a protein-making template; other RNAs help build, regulate or carry out cellular processes.
records.summary: RNA uses ribose and usually uracil in place of DNA’s thymine. It is often single-stranded but can fold through internal pairing. Messenger RNA carries a coding template; ribosomal RNA contributes to ribosome structure and catalysis; transfer RNA brings amino acids; regulatory RNAs influence other molecules. Many nuclear messages receive a 5-prime cap and poly(A) tail and have introns removed by splicing before translation, but these features are not universal to all RNAs. Ribosomes read a coding sequence in codons to produce a polypeptide; processing, folding and localization follow.

After successful delivery, a supplied ordinary mRNA can be translated at cytoplasmic ribosomes; that translation step does not require the message to enter the nucleus. Supplying a message, measuring endogenous tumor RNA and demonstrating nuclear DNA modification are separate observations. records.name: Gene
records.tldr: A gene is a DNA region that produces a functional RNA message. Some messages encode proteins; others work as RNA.
records.summary: A protein-coding gene supplies RNA that can be translated into a polypeptide, while a noncoding RNA gene produces a functional RNA. Promoters and other regulatory regions influence transcription in a cell-dependent context. One gene can have several transcript versions. Exons are retained regions of a specified processed transcript and can include untranslated sequence; introns are removed by splicing. Coding sequence is the translated part of a coding message. A gene name alone does not specify a transcript, coding interval or protein product.

records.name: Protein
records.tldr: Proteins are amino-acid products that provide structure, catalysis, transport and signaling. A detected fragment and a complete working protein are different findings.
records.summary: Amino acids join through peptide bonds into polypeptide chains; linked amino acids are residues. Peptide and protein usage overlaps without a universal length boundary. A protein may contain one or several chains, folded domains and flexible regions. Processing, chemical modifications, localization, production and degradation affect its form and behavior. Genes specify coding templates, but a DNA or RNA finding does not measure the resulting protein’s intact structure or activity.

Many mass-spectrometry workflows digest proteins into peptides: a shared detected peptide cannot distinguish every full-length form. A candidate peptide sequence also does not establish its display by HLA. Separate assays address amount, location, intact form, function and antigen presentation.

records.name: Enzyme
records.tldr: An enzyme speeds a chemical reaction and is reused through its reaction cycle. Binding to an enzyme does not by itself show that the reaction or a cell response changed.
records.summary: Catalysis lowers a reaction’s activation barrier without supplying an unlimited energy source. Most familiar enzymes are proteins, while some RNAs also catalyze reactions. Active-site interactions help chemistry; other binding sites can regulate activity. Binding, catalytic rate, substrate preference and activity in a cell are different properties. An inhibitor can act through the active site or another mechanism, and turnover rates are not one universal number.

records.summary: Transcription makes RNA from DNA; translation reads a coding message in codons to make a polypeptide. This information-flow description does not require every RNA to become protein. A promoter recruits transcription machinery. Enhancers influence transcription through regulatory interactions that can span distant DNA positions. Transcription factors recognize sequence features and participate in regulation. Chromatin, RNA processing and turnover, translation, protein processing and degradation all influence the eventual product. A transcript’s frame and reference context matter when interpreting a sequence change.

records.name: RNA splicing
records.tldr: RNA processing removes introns and joins retained exons. Different processing choices can produce different messages without changing the underlying gene sequence.
records.summary:
Splicing processes an initial RNA transcript. Exons are retained in a specified product and may contain untranslated sequence; introns are removed. For many nuclear pre-mRNAs, a spliceosome made of RNA and proteins recognizes boundary and regulatory sequences. The donor site starts an intron and the acceptor site ends it. Alternative choices yield transcript isoforms; a variant can alter exon inclusion, intron retention or use of a cryptic site. Exon skipping is not automatically a frameshift: the coding sequence and resulting joins matter. An altered message may undergo nonsense-mediated decay or produce a changed protein, but neither outcome follows from a prediction alone.

Cancer-associated splicing changes can arise through altered RNA-processing factors or their expression. SF3B1, SRSF2, U2AF1 and ZRSR2 illustrate studied factors; AR-V7 and BCL2L1 illustrate named transcript contexts. The linked review describes disease-specific mechanisms and therapeutic research. An altered transcript alone does not establish an intact abnormal protein, immune presentation, a therapeutic dependency or patient benefit. Free-drug development and a conjugated payload also require their own construct-specific evidence.

records.name: Mutation
records.tldr: A DNA variant describes a sequence change relative to a reference. Its origin, effect and clinical importance require separate evidence.
records.summary: A single-nucleotide substitution changes one base. Insertions and deletions change sequence length; copy-number and structural alterations affect larger regions and can overlap in category. In a specified coding transcript, missense changes alter an amino acid, synonymous changes preserve it, and nonsense changes introduce a stop. A net coding indel not divisible by three can shift the reading frame; an indel outside coding sequence is not automatically a frameshift. Transcript and reference versions determine the description.

records.tldr: A ligand binds a molecular partner. Binding does not necessarily activate a receptor or prove that a treatment will help.

A bound ligand may activate a specified response, oppose another ligand, or show no effect in that assay. Some targeting ligands localize a payload. An accessible binding address need not be a cancer’s growth driver; delivery, intracellular action and clinical benefit require further evidence.

records.name: Receptor
records.tldr: Receptors connect molecular recognition to a cellular response through several mechanisms. Their presence and their activity are separate findings.
records.summary: Receptors can be on the surface or inside a cell. Ligand-gated ion channels regulate ion passage; G-protein-coupled receptors act through G proteins; enzyme-linked receptors can contain an enzyme or recruit a separate one. Intracellular nuclear receptors can regulate transcription with cellular partners. A surface signal can ultimately alter genes, while nuclear-receptor family membership does not fix every molecule permanently in the nucleus or require every effect to use new transcription.

records.name: Agonist and antagonist
records.tldr: Agonists promote a specified receptor response; antagonists oppose agonist action. The labels depend on the measured system, and strong binding does not necessarily mean strong activation.

A partial agonist has lower activating capacity; its observed maximum depends on receptor amount and amplification and is not defined by giving a smaller dose of a full agonist. Competing partial agonists can reduce a full agonist’s response when they replace it. A neutral antagonist opposes agonist action without changing agonist-independent baseline activity; an inverse agonist reduces that activity when it is measurable. Antagonism need not use the agonist’s binding site.

records.tldr: A signaling pathway connects an input to cellular changes. Real pathways branch, interact and feed back, so one changed marker does not describe the whole network.

records.name: Variant allele frequency (VAF)
records.tldr: Variant allele frequency is the fraction of informative reads or molecules that support a variant under a test’s definition. It is not directly the fraction of cancer cells.
records.summary: Read-based VAF divides variant-supporting reads by informative reads at the locus. Some assays instead report a molecule-based measure, so keep the laboratory’s definition. Tumor purity, local allele-specific copy number, ploidy, subclonal mixture and assay behavior affect the value. VAF alone cannot assign zygosity, variant origin, the number of clones or a cancer-cell percentage. Changes over time in plasma also require attention to specimen and non-tumor DNA contributors.

records.name: Genome-wide loss of heterozygosity (gLOH)
records.tldr: This assay-defined score summarizes genomic regions that lost previously different allelic information. It can reflect a past repair defect, including changes that preserve total DNA copy count.
records.summary:
Loss of heterozygosity means loss of previously distinct allelic information at a locus. It can accompany copy loss or occur with a copy-neutral allelic change; tumor purity and ploidy complicate inference. Genome-wide loss of heterozygosity summarizes affected interrogated regions according to the assay’s definition. It is studied as a genomic scar associated with some homologous-recombination-repair defects, rather than a direct measurement of present repair function.

The threshold belongs to the assay and setting. ARIEL2 part 1 prespecified 14 percent or more as LOH high in its ovarian-cancer analysis; this does not establish a universal cutoff. Pan-cancer studies found elevated gLOH associated with biallelic BRCA1/2 alterations and with a core set of other repair-gene alterations, with effects differing by cancer context. Monoallelic calls and an HRR-gene-list label are not interchangeable with those findings. TP53 loss was independently associated with gLOH in the Westphalen analysis.

In 3,476 prostate tumors, Chung and colleagues found BRCA1/2, ATR and FANCA alterations associated with high gLOH, while CDK12-altered tumors, about 6 percent of that cohort, were infrequently gLOH high. The study did not correlate these findings with clinical outcomes. Such associations support gene-specific biological questions; they do not establish an individual patient’s drug benefit or current treatment eligibility.

Tumour sequencing and clinical hereditary testing answer different questions. The historical TRITON2 study reported similar objective response rates in germline- and somatic-BRCA groups in its enrolled prostate-cancer population; that result is not a current treatment-access rule or evidence that a negative hereditary assay excludes acquired tumour variants.

A local LOH state and a genome-wide LOH score have different scope. In an idealised informative A/B region, 1+1 and 2+0 both total two copies, but only 2+0 loses one sequence version. A total-copy profile alone cannot distinguish them. Allele-aware inputs and purity/ploidy assumptions constrain the call; a genome-wide score does not identify the retained sequence, phase a mutation or directly measure current gene function.

records.name: Gene amplification and copy-number change
records.tldr: Cancer cells often have extra copies of a growth gene (amplification) or have lost copies of a protective one (deletion), rather than a spelling change within the gene. Extra copies of HER2 or MYCN are classic examples that change treatment.
records.summary: Amplification (detected by FISH, ISH or NGS copy-number calls) can increase gene dosage and expression: HER2 in breast and gastric cancer, MYCN in high-risk neuroblastoma, MET amplification as a resistance route to EGFR inhibitors, CCNE1 in ovarian and gastric cancer, MDM2 in liposarcoma, CDK4 in glioma. Deletions remove tumour suppressors: del(17p)/TP53 in CLL and myeloma (predicting chemo-resistance), CDKN2A/B in glioma (defining grade 4), MTAP (creating a PRMT5 vulnerability), 9p21 loss linked to immunotherapy resistance. Loss of heterozygosity and larger chromosome changes contribute to some method-defined genomic-scar scores. Their clinical interpretation depends on the exact test, cancer and treatment setting; a copy state alone does not establish current repair function or drug benefit.

notes: Total copy count, allele identity, RNA abundance and protein activity are separate measurements. Purity, ploidy and the assay’s definition affect copy calls. Fehrmann and colleagues related copy number to expression after modelling shared transcriptional components in large datasets; that association does not promise a fixed protein increase, target dependence or treatment benefit in a particular tumour.
Total copy number counts copies of a region; allele-specific copy number estimates the contributions of the distinguishable sequence versions A and B.
1+1 is two copies with both versions; 1+0 is one copy with LOH (deletion); 2+0 is copy-neutral LOH (two copies, one version); 2+1 is three copies with both versions retained.
LOH is not synonymous with deletion: copy-neutral LOH can follow loss plus duplication or recombination; a gain does not necessarily erase either version.

Major and minor counts are the larger and smaller allelic contributions; minor of zero supports LOH under the model; they do not identify parental origin or assign a mutation to a copy; phasing needs suitable evidence.
Local copy count differs from ploidy; relative signal can fit different purity and ploidy pairs; fractional counts can reflect mixture or subclonal states.

Methods combine relative coverage with allele balance at informative heterozygous sites, segment the genome and fit states; a matched normal helps; a total-copy profile alone cannot separate 1+1 from 2+0; homozygous sites are uninformative.
Copy state does not establish phase, gene inactivity, expression, dependency or drug response; bulk fits can hide subpopulations and unsampled lesions.
Fictional teaching exercise: Two A copies and no B copies under an adequate model is copy-neutral LOH: not deleted and not proven inactive.

Reanalysis alone needs no tissue. Low purity, uninformative sites and ambiguous fits limit inference; amplification and functional-loss criteria are method-specific.

records.name: Immunoglobulin and T-cell receptor clonality testing
records.tldr: Receptor-gene patterns can provide evidence of a clonal lymphocyte population. The result must be interpreted with the tissue findings and does not diagnose cancer by itself.
records.summary:
Developing lymphocytes rearrange antigen-receptor genes. Shared rearrangements can support common ancestry, but a detected clonal pattern is not synonymous with malignancy, and a negative assay does not exclude it. Sampling, reactive expansions, multiple alleles, primer coverage and technical artifacts affect interpretation. The number of peaks is not a direct count of clones.

The European BIOMED-2 collaboration standardised the assay into 107 primers in 18 multiplex tubes covering the immunoglobulin heavy chain in two configurations, the kappa and lambda light chains, the T-cell receptor beta, gamma and delta loci, and the BCL1-IGH and BCL2-IGH translocations, read by heteroduplex analysis or fragment sizing. The EuroClonality-NGS successor sequences the amplicons instead of sizing them, which both improves resolution and produces a patient-specific sequence that can be followed afterwards as a residual disease marker.

The assay is most often ordered where morphology and immunohistochemistry disagree or where the sample is small: a skin biopsy in suspected cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, a gastric biopsy in suspected MALT lymphoma, a marrow with an ambiguous infiltrate, or a lymph node with an atypical but not clearly malignant population.

records.name: DNA methylation arrays and beta values (450k, EPIC)

DNA methylation in promoters typically represses transcription and is a stable record of cell identity, which is why methylation classifiers work for brain tumours and why methylation adds tissue-of-origin information to expression.

records.name: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC)
aka: ER negative PR negative HER2 negative
records.tldr: A breast cancer classified as oestrogen receptor-negative, progesterone receptor-negative and HER2-negative by the relevant tests. Negative test categories do not mean that every receptor molecule is absent.
records.summary:
TNBC is defined by negative ER, PR and HER2 test classifications: ER and PR nuclear staining below 1 percent, and HER2-negative results under the applicable IHC/ISH algorithm. These classifications do not establish the complete absence of receptor molecules. It is biologically heterogeneous (including distinct RNA expression profiles and histologies), often TP53-mutant, frequently HRD-positive (11 to 17% germline BRCA1/2 by cohort), and can express TROP2. Expression and cellular composition vary between tumours and need the sampled tissue and assay context. Relapses cluster in the first three years and favour visceral and brain metastases.

The standard of care changed three times in six years. KEYNOTE-522 (2020-21) made pembrolizumab plus carboplatin-containing chemotherapy before surgery, continued after, the standard for stage II-III disease, with a 4.9-point overall survival gain at five years (86.6% against 81.7%). OlympiA (2021) added adjuvant olaparib for germline BRCA carriers with residual disease. In metastatic disease, pembrolizumab-chemotherapy (CPS ≥10) was joined by the TROP2 ADCs: sacituzumab govitecan (ASCENT, reported in 2021; first-line ASCENT-03/04 2026) and datopotamab deruxtecan (TROPION-Breast02, first-line PD-1-ineligible, 2026, with an overall survival benefit), while trastuzumab deruxtecan has a specified advanced-breast HER2-low use after prior chemotherapy. The separate HR-positive ultralow use after endocrine therapy does not extend to TNBC. The EGFR×HER3 bispecific ADC iza-bren posted the first positive phase 3 for a bispecific ADC in pretreated TNBC in February 2026.

What remains unsolved: residual disease after KEYNOTE-522 (RCB II-III) still carries a high relapse risk (before immunotherapy, ten-year relapse-free survival was 55% for RCB-II and 23% for RCB-III, Symmans 2017); ADC sequencing (TOP1-payload cross-resistance) is unstudied; PD-L1-negative early disease has immunotherapy proven only in KEYNOTE-522's unselected population; brain metastases; and response and resistance within mesenchymal or claudin-low patterns need setting-specific evidence. Research directions include ADC + IO first line, de-escalation guided by TILs and pCR, ctDNA-guided escalation, TROP2 PET selection, next-generation ADCs with non-TOP1 or dual payloads, and personalised vaccines in the adjuvant setting.

Research expression subtyping, receptor tests, histology and inherited-risk results describe different axes. The 2016 TNBCtype-4 refinement retained BL1, BL2, M and LAR after investigating immune and stromal contributions to the older IM/MSL signals. A research label alone does not establish treatment sensitivity. Prospective strategies using other classifiers retain their own assay, matching rules, population and regimens.

How common it is, world and United States. No registry publishes a world count of triple-negative disease; the share has to be applied to breast cancer as a whole. The IARC breast fact sheet, served today with the GLOBOCAN 2024 estimates, gives 2,434,087 new breast cancers a year (the second commonest cancer, age-standardised rate 47.8 per 100,000) and 693,660 deaths (fourth, 12.9 per 100,000), with 45.1 percent of cases in Asia, 22.3 percent in Europe, 13.2 percent in Northern America, 9.3 percent in Africa and 9.0 percent in Latin America and the Caribbean. The triple-negative share in registries with receptor data runs from 8.4 percent of 1,151,724 US cases in 2010 to 2014 (Scott 2019) through 10.8 percent of all US cases, including those of unknown subtype, in SEER 21, 2019 to 2023 (the SEER subtype fact sheet), 12.2 percent of cases with known status in 2010 (Howlader 2014) and 12 percent in 2012 to 2016 (Howard and Olopade 2021), to around 15 percent on the Cancer Research UK patient page and 17 percent of 15,204 women treated at NCCN centres in 2000 to 2006 (Lin 2012). Applied to 2.4 million, a share of 10 to 15 percent would be about 240,000 to 370,000 people a year; that is arithmetic on the figures above, not a published count. In the United States the age-adjusted rate of hormone receptor-negative, HER2-negative breast cancer is 14.3 per 100,000 women a year against 132.5 for all breast cancer (SEER 21, 2019 to 2023), and 321,910 new female breast cancers of all subtypes are projected for 2026.

Who gets it. Age: triple-negative tumours are diagnosed younger than hormone receptor-positive tumours. Women under 40 had 1.53 times the odds of the triple-negative phenotype in the California registry (Bauer 2007) and 1.95 times the odds relative to women aged 50 to 64 in US Cancer Statistics (Scott 2019); Howlader found triple-negative patients 10 to 30 percent less likely to be diagnosed at older ages and 6.4 to 20 times more likely to present with high-grade disease; Cancer Research UK says the type develops more often in women under 40. Ethnicity: in SEER 21 (2019 to 2023) the rate of hormone receptor-negative, HER2-negative disease is 25.7 per 100,000 in non-Hispanic Black women against 13.0 in non-Hispanic White, 12.5 in Hispanic, 11.4 in American Indian and Alaska Native and 10.5 in Asian and Pacific Islander women, roughly a two-fold difference; non-Hispanic Black women had 2.27 times the odds of a triple-negative diagnosis in 2010 to 2014 (Scott 2019); the basal-like subtype was found in 39 percent of premenopausal African American women against 16 percent of non-African American women in the Carolina Breast Cancer Study (Carey 2006); and in 507 women in Nigeria and Senegal, triple-negative disease (basal-like 27 percent plus unclassified 28 percent) predominated, with a mean age of 44.8 (Huo 2009). In the UK, the POSH cohort of women diagnosed at 40 or under found triple-negative tumours in 26.1 percent of Black against 18.6 percent of White patients (Copson 2014), and an analysis of 116,500 women in England (2013 to 2018) found greater adjusted odds of ER-negative, high-grade and high-stage tumours in ethnic minority women, most marked in Black African and Black Caribbean women (Gathani 2021). Even after adjustment for stage, treatment delay and socioeconomic factors, African American women with triple-negative disease remain nearly twice as likely to die of it (Howard and Olopade 2021). Inherited risk: 57.1 percent of breast cancers in BRCA1 carriers were triple-negative against 23.3 percent in BRCA2 carriers and 13.8 percent in non-carriers (Atchley 2008); in 6,893 carriers the triple-negative share fell with age at diagnosis in BRCA1 and rose in BRCA2 carriers, and medullary tumours were BRCA1-related (Mavaddat 2012). Looked at from the other side, 14.6 percent of 1,824 triple-negative patients unselected for family history carried a deleterious mutation in one of 17 genes, 8.5 percent BRCA1, 2.7 percent BRCA2 and 1.2 percent PALB2 (Couch 2015); a prospective US registry found 15.4 percent with BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations, 27.6 percent among those diagnosed at 50 or under, 11.4 percent at 51 to 60 and 4.9 percent at 61 or over (Sharma 2014); and 12 percent of 2,733 UK women with breast cancer at 40 or under carried a BRCA mutation (Copson 2018). Cancer Research UK puts the lifetime breast cancer risk of a BRCA1 or BRCA2 carrier at 45 to 65 percent by age 70, with about 1 in 450 women carrying a mutation; PALB2 carries a relative risk of 7.18 and a 53 percent risk to age 80 (Yang 2020).

United Kingdom (Cancer Research UK, drawing on the four national registries). Breast cancer is the commonest cancer, with 59,413 new cases a year (2019 and 2021 to 2022), about 59,000 in females and 420 in males, 15 percent of all cancers; a quarter are diagnosed at 75 or over; incidence rates have risen 20 percent since the early 1990s and are projected to fall 1 percent by 2038 to 2040 while the count rises to about 70,300 a year; incidence rates are lower in the Asian and Black ethnic groups than the White group in England (2013 to 2017), which sits beside the higher triple-negative share in Black women noted above. There are about 11,200 deaths a year (2022 to 2024), the fourth commonest cause of cancer death and the second in women; mortality rates have fallen 46 percent since the early 1970s. In England in 2022, 85 percent of cases with a known stage were stage I or II; in 2019, 53 percent were diagnosed through an urgent suspected cancer referral, 32 percent through screening and 4 percent after an emergency presentation. About 23 percent of UK breast cancers are judged preventable, 8 percent attributed to alcohol and 1 percent to ionising radiation. Cancer Research UK does not publish a separate UK incidence count for triple-negative disease; the around 15 percent share on its patient page, and the 20 percent share in the young-onset POSH cohort (558 of 2,733), are the UK figures found for this record.

Risk factors that separate triple-negative from other breast cancers. Reproduction runs the other way from hormone receptor-positive disease: in 23,353 cases and 71,072 controls pooled across 31 studies, parous women had a lower risk of every luminal and HER2-enriched-like subtype but a higher risk of triple-negative disease immediately after a birth (odds ratio 3.12 for multiparous women right after their last birth), attenuating over decades (Jung 2022); in African American women parity raised triple-negative risk (odds ratio 1.37) while breastfeeding lowered ER-negative risk (0.81), and ER-negative risk rose with each birth in women who had not breastfed (1.68 for four or more births) (Palmer 2014). Cancer Research UK's summary that triple-negative disease is not associated with parity, from an older meta-analysis, is recorded beside these newer pooled analyses. Obesity: triple-negative cases were more often obese than hormone receptor-positive cases (odds ratio 1.20 case-case, 1.24 case-control), a signal confined to premenopausal women (1.43) in an 11-study meta-analysis (Pierobon 2013), and 1.89 in an Atlanta case series (Trivers 2009); Cancer Research UK notes the postmenopausal body-mass effect is largely limited to ER- and PR-positive tumours (adult weight gain raised ER- and PR-negative risk by 34 percent against 133 percent for positive tumours). Age at first birth and at menarche, and oral contraceptive or HRT use, are associated mainly with hormone receptor-positive tumours (CRUK risk page). A first-degree relative with breast cancer doubles breast cancer risk of any type, and the germline factors above (BRCA1 above all, then PALB2 and BRCA2) are the strongest known triple-negative risk factors. What is shared with all breast cancer: alcohol (8 percent of UK cases), ionising radiation (1 percent) and breast density (3 to 5 times the risk in the most dense breasts).

How it presents. Symptoms are those of any breast cancer: a lump or thickening in the breast or armpit, a change in size, shape or feel, skin puckering, dimpling, a rash or redness, fluid from the nipple, or a nipple that turns in (Cancer Research UK triple-negative and symptoms pages). What differs is the route and the tempo. Triple-negative tumours are less often found by a screening mammogram (29 percent against 48 percent of hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative tumours in NCCN centres) and present with a higher tumour category but are less likely to involve the lymph nodes (Lin 2012); they are over-represented among interval cancers, which appear between screens and carry worse prognostic features than screen-detected cancers (Houssami 2017); and they are more often high grade (Howlader 2014). Relapse is early: in 1,601 Toronto patients the triple-negative group had 2.6 times the hazard of distant recurrence and 3.2 times the hazard of death within five years but not afterwards, with the risk of distant recurrence peaking at about three years and falling rapidly (Dent 2007); recurrence and death rates were higher only in the first three years in the MD Anderson neoadjuvant series, which also found more visceral and fewer bone relapses (Liedtke 2008); and in 116 patients with metastatic disease treated in 2000 to 2006, 46 percent developed brain metastases before death and median survival from the metastatic diagnosis was 13.3 months (Lin 2008), a figure that the later trials in the treatment rows have moved. NICE NG12 (1.4) asks GPs to refer on the suspected cancer pathway anyone aged 30 or over with an unexplained breast lump, anyone 50 or over with discharge, retraction or other change in one nipple, and to consider it for skin changes or an unexplained axillary lump at 30 or over.

How it is diagnosed. In the UK the GP refers to a one-stop breast clinic for triple assessment: examination, mammogram, ultrasound and a needle core (or vacuum-assisted) biopsy, with axillary ultrasound and needle biopsy of any abnormal node (Cancer Research UK tests page). NICE NG101 (1.3.1 to 1.3.4) requires ER, PR and HER2 status to be assessed simultaneously on every invasive breast cancer at the initial histopathological diagnosis, by standardised, quality-assured immunohistochemistry reported quantitatively, and recorded at the preoperative and postoperative multidisciplinary meetings. Triple-negative is then a laboratory definition: ER negative when fewer than 1 percent of tumour nuclei stain, PR likewise, with 1 to 10 percent reported as a new ER Low Positive category on which endocrine benefit is uncertain (ASCO/CAP 2020, Allison); HER2 negative when immunohistochemistry is 0 or 1+, or 2+ with no amplification on in situ hybridisation (ASCO/CAP 2018, Wolff). The 2023 ASCO-CAP update kept those categories but added a reporting comment because the difference between HER2 0 and 1+ now decides eligibility for trastuzumab deruxtecan (Wolff 2023). NG101 defines triple-negative simply as ER, PR and HER2 each scored negative under local multidisciplinary team rules. Where the receptors are low rather than absent the behaviour is the same: ER 1 to 10 percent tumours matched ER-negative tumours for germline BRCA prevalence, response and survival in a US registry (Yoder 2022) and in an Italian series (Dieci 2021), and Sweden treats ER 1 to 9 percent HER2-negative tumours as triple-negative, with 9.9 percent of 5,655 such cancers in 2008 to 2020 falling in that band (Acs 2024). Breast MRI is not routine before surgery but is offered when the extent of disease is unclear, when breast density defeats mammography, or to size an invasive lobular cancer (NG101 1.2). Staging tests beyond the breast and axilla, where the stage or symptoms warrant, are CT, bone scan, liver ultrasound or PET-CT, and blood tests including CA 15-3 which cannot diagnose or direct treatment on its own (Cancer Research UK tests page). NG101 (1.3.6) adds one test that applies to this subtype alone: offer germline BRCA1 and BRCA2 testing to women under 50 with triple-negative breast cancer, including those with no family history.

What the pathologist sees. Most triple-negative cancers are invasive carcinomas of no special type (the term the 2019 WHO classification, 5th edition, uses for what was called ductal carcinoma) of grade 3, with a high proliferation index: the Swedish cohort's median Ki-67 was 63 percent in ER-zero and 60 percent in ER-low tumours, and 80.8 percent of ER-zero tumours were grade III (Acs 2024). By gene expression, 78.6 percent of triple-negative tumours are basal-like and 21.4 percent belong to other intrinsic subtypes, while 31.5 percent of basal-like tumours are not triple-negative (Prat 2013); basal-like tumours share many molecular features with high-grade serous ovarian cancer, and TP53 is the mutation that recurs across them (TCGA 2012). Within the triple-negative group, Lehmann's 2011 analysis of 587 cases found six expression subtypes (basal-like 1 and 2, immunomodulatory, mesenchymal, mesenchymal stem-like and luminal androgen receptor), refined in 2016 to four tumour-intrinsic subtypes once the immunomodulatory and stem-like signals were traced to infiltrating lymphocytes and stroma; Burstein's four (luminal androgen receptor, mesenchymal, basal-like immunosuppressed and basal-like immune-activated) overlap them. Each has a page linked from this record. The WHO classification also names special histological types that are usually triple-negative: metaplastic carcinoma (70.3 percent triple-negative in 2,451 US cases, Ong 2018), carcinoma with medullary pattern (no longer a separate type in the 5th edition, Thomas 2023; Cserni 2020), adenoid cystic carcinoma (95 percent localised at diagnosis, 15-year relative survival 91.4 percent, Ghabach 2010), apocrine carcinoma (ER and PR negative, androgen receptor positive, Vranic 2013) and secretory carcinoma (ETV6-NTRK3 fusion in 92 percent, Tognon 2002). Rare subtypes together are 5 to 10 percent of triple-negative cancers (Thomas 2023), and the European Working Group for Breast Screening Pathology concludes that patients with the indolent pure forms (classical adenoid cystic, low-grade adenosquamous, fibromatosis-like metaplastic, secretory, acinic cell, tall cell with reversed polarity) are unlikely to benefit from chemotherapy (Cserni 2021). Stromal tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes are scored on the biopsy, and PD-L1 combined positive score is tested when metastatic treatment is planned (the glossary terms carry the thresholds).

How it is staged. The TNM 8th edition (2017) is the usual system in the UK, and Cancer Research UK sets it out in plain words. T1 is 2 cm or less (T1mi 0.1 cm or less, T1a to 0.5 cm, T1b to 1 cm, T1c to 2 cm), T2 over 2 to 5 cm, T3 over 5 cm, T4 into the chest wall (a), skin (b), both (c) or inflammatory carcinoma (d). Nodes are staged clinically (cN) before any treatment and pathologically (pN) from the sentinel node or clearance: pN1 one to three axillary nodes (pN1mi micrometastases 0.2 to 2 mm), pN2 four to nine, pN3 ten or more or infraclavicular, or axillary plus internal mammary, or supraclavicular nodes. Stage 1A is T1 N0; 1B adds micrometastases; 2A is T0 to T1 N1 or T2 N0; 2B is T2 N1 or T3 N0; 3A is N2 with T0 to T3 or T3 N1; 3B is T4 with N0 to N2; 3C is any N3; stage 4 is any M1. The American Joint Committee on Cancer's 8th edition kept this anatomic stage but added a prognostic stage that folds grade, ER, PR and HER2 status (and, for some hormone receptor-positive tumours, a low Oncotype DX score) into the stage group (Giuliano 2017); in a 3,327-patient MD Anderson cohort the prognostic stage moved 29.5 percent of patients up and 28.1 percent down, and predicted disease-specific survival better than the anatomic stage (C index 0.84 against 0.74), with the same result in 54,727 Californian patients (Weiss 2018). Because grade 3 and receptor negativity count against a tumour, a triple-negative cancer generally carries a higher prognostic than anatomic stage; the UK pathway pages quote the anatomic stage. When chemotherapy is given before surgery, as it is for most stage II and III triple-negative disease, the response at surgery (pathological complete response or residual cancer burden) becomes the stronger prognostic marker (Cortazar 2014; Symmans 2017; the glossary terms).

Screening and prevention. There is no screening test for triple-negative disease as such. The NHS Breast Screening Programme invites everyone registered as female from age 50 (first invitation between 50 and 53) every three years until their 71st birthday, and women 71 or over can ask for screening (NHS). Because triple-negative tumours arrive younger and grow between rounds, a smaller share is screen-detected (Lin 2012; Houssami 2017), which is one reason the family history pathway matters here. NICE CG164 sets the UK rules: GPs refer to a specialist breast or genetics clinic on defined family patterns, and clinicians should seek genetics advice for families containing triple-negative breast cancer under 40, Jewish ancestry, sarcoma under 45 or glioma; genetic testing is offered when the combined BRCA1 and BRCA2 carrier probability is 10 percent or more (calculated with CanRisk, formerly BOADICEA, or the Manchester score); known BRCA1 or BRCA2 carriers are offered annual MRI from 30 to 49 and annual mammography from 40 to 69, TP53 carriers MRI from 20, and MRI is not offered to carriers aged 50 to 69 unless the breasts are dense. In the UK MARIBS study of 649 women at high familial risk, MRI sensitivity was 77 percent against 40 percent for mammography, 92 against 23 percent in BRCA1 carriers (Leach 2005). Risk-reducing surgery: bilateral mastectomy cut breast cancer risk by about 90 percent in BRCA1 and BRCA2 carriers in PROSE (1.9 percent against 48.7 percent over a mean 6.4 years; Rebbeck 2004) and pooled relative risk 0.114 in a 15-study meta-analysis, with contralateral mastectomy 0.072 and salpingo-oophorectomy 0.552 for breast cancer overall (Li 2016), though a prospective study of 3,722 carriers found oophorectomy did not lower breast cancer risk in BRCA1 carriers (hazard ratio 0.96) (Kotsopoulos 2017). CG164 restricts risk-reducing mastectomy to a small proportion of women from high-risk families, managed by a multidisciplinary team with genetic counselling, verified family history and reconstruction options discussed. Chemoprevention has a gap that matters for this subtype: NICE offers tamoxifen (premenopausal) or anastrozole (postmenopausal) for five years to women at high risk, and considers them at moderate risk, but tamoxifen had no effect on invasive ER-negative breast cancer in IBIS-I (hazard ratio 1.05 over 16 years; Cuzick 2015) or NSABP P-1 (Fisher 1998), and anastrozole's 49 percent reduction in IBIS-II came from ER-positive disease (54 percent fewer invasive ER-positive cancers, no significant effect on ER-negative cancer; Cuzick 2020); Cancer Research UK says the trial evidence is unclear for women with gene changes. One observational signal runs the other way: tamoxifen after a first breast cancer was associated with a lower contralateral breast cancer risk in BRCA1 (hazard ratio 0.38) and BRCA2 (0.33) carriers regardless of the first tumour's ER status (Phillips 2013). Breastfeeding is the modifiable factor with a specific ER-negative signal (Palmer 2014), and keeping a healthy weight and being physically active are the general measures Cancer Research UK names.

notes: What does triple-negative actually mean? The tested invasive cancer is classified as ER-negative and PR-negative, each below 1 percent nuclear staining, and HER2-negative under the relevant IHC/ISH algorithm. Retain the specimen, score and test-validity information. These test categories do not establish that every receptor molecule is absent or that the cell has no other receptors. ER 1 to 10 percent is ER Low Positive; limited endocrine-benefit evidence and overlap in some cohort features do not make it ER-negative (ASCO/CAP 2020 and 2023).

How common is it? About 10.8 percent of all US breast cancers (SEER 21, 2019 to 2023) and around 15 percent on Cancer Research UK's page; roughly 12 percent in earlier US series (Howlader 2014). It is diagnosed younger: women under 40 have about 1.5 to 2 times the odds of a triple-negative diagnosis (Bauer 2007; Scott 2019).

Why is it more common in Black women? In the United States the rate is 25.7 per 100,000 non-Hispanic Black women against 13.0 for non-Hispanic White women (SEER 21), and in the UK POSH cohort 26.1 percent of Black against 18.6 percent of White young patients had triple-negative tumours (Copson 2014). Reproductive patterns (parity without breastfeeding raises ER-negative risk in African American women, Palmer 2014), ancestry and access all contribute; the causes are not settled (Howard and Olopade 2021).

Should I have a genetic test? NICE says yes for women under 50 with triple-negative disease even without a family history (NG101 1.3.6), and UK mainstream criteria extend testing to all triple-negative disease under 60 (Evans 2024); about 11 percent of unselected triple-negative patients carry a BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation and 14.6 percent a mutation in one of 17 genes (Couch 2015). The result changes surgery options, opens olaparib after chemotherapy for high-risk early disease (NICE TA886) and matters for relatives.

Is it more dangerous than other breast cancers? Stage for stage, survival is lower: 78.7 percent five-year relative survival against 95.8 percent for hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative disease in SEER, but 92.8 percent when found while localised. The risk of relapse is concentrated in the first three to five years and is low afterwards (Dent 2007), and a pathological complete response to chemotherapy before surgery carries an excellent outlook (Liedtke 2008; Cortazar 2014).

Why did my treatment start with chemotherapy rather than surgery? For tumours over 2 cm or with node involvement, chemotherapy with pembrolizumab is given first because the response at surgery predicts relapse and directs what follows, and because it raised five-year survival from 81.7 to 86.6 percent in KEYNOTE-522 (Schmid 2024). NICE recommends a platinum, a taxane and an anthracycline in that setting (NG101 1.8, 2025) and pembrolizumab with it (TA851).

Does hormone therapy or tamoxifen have any role? Hormone receptor-negative breast cancer generally does not respond to endocrine treatment. ER Low Positive is a separate positive category with limited benefit data and needs its own clinical interpretation. As prevention, tamoxifen and anastrozole reduced ER-positive but not ER-negative breast cancer in the prevention trials (Cuzick 2015; Fisher 1998; Cuzick 2020), although tamoxifen after a first cancer was associated with fewer contralateral cancers in BRCA carriers (Phillips 2013).

Will screening pick it up? The NHS invites women from 50 to 71 every three years (NHS). Triple-negative cancers are less often screen-detected (29 percent against 48 percent, Lin 2012) because they arise younger and grow between rounds. Known BRCA carriers are offered annual MRI from 30 and mammography from 40 (NICE CG164); anyone with a new breast change should see a GP without waiting for the next screen.

What are the subtypes I might read about? Gene expression divides triple-negative disease into basal-like 1 and 2, mesenchymal and luminal androgen receptor tumours (Lehmann 2016), which respond differently to chemotherapy (pathological complete response 41 percent for basal-like 1, 18 percent for basal-like 2, 29 percent for luminal androgen receptor) but are not used to choose treatment in the NHS. Special histological types such as adenoid cystic and secretory carcinoma are triple-negative but indolent and may need no chemotherapy (Cserni 2021). Each has a page linked from this record.

What is HER2-low and why can it matter within a HER2-negative report? IHC 1+ or IHC 2+/ISH-negative is a HER2-low category used in specified studies and labelling. DESTINY-Breast04 included hormone receptor-negative disease after chemotherapy. The current U.S. T-DXd low-expression breast use requires an advanced-disease setting and specified prior treatment; the separate ultralow use after endocrine therapy requires HR-positive disease. A staining result alone does not establish all the clinical requirements or promise a response.

Metastatic samples in breast_msk_2018 (85 of 176) and the 173-gene METABRIC panel make cross-cohort comparison approximate; TMB on the MSK panel is reported as a mutation count, not a per-megabase rate.

Receptor classification, grade and stage describe different features. Triple-negative refers to the ER, PR and HER2 test results; grade describes microscopic features, and stage describes extent together with the factors in the applicable staging system. A grade does not replace receptor testing or establish an individual prognosis. ER 1 to 10 percent is ER Low Positive under ASCO/CAP criteria, with limited endocrine-benefit evidence; it should not be relabelled ER-negative from an average cohort comparison. Trial entry rules require the actual protocol.

standardOfCare.setting: Stage I (T1a-b N0)
standardOfCare.approach: Surgery ± radiation; chemotherapy for ≥T1c; stage I tumours with TILs of 50% or more had 94% 5-year distant relapse-free survival without chemotherapy in a pooled 1,966-patient analysis (Leon-Ferre 2024). De-escalation trials ongoing.

standardOfCare.setting: Stage II-III
standardOfCare.approach: Neoadjuvant pembrolizumab + carboplatin/paclitaxel → AC/EC, surgery, adjuvant pembrolizumab (KEYNOTE-522). Germline BRCA + residual disease: olaparib 1 year (OlympiA). Residual disease without BRCA: capecitabine (CREATE-X). Radiation per stage.

standardOfCare.approach: Pembrolizumab + chemotherapy (KEYNOTE-355) or sacituzumab govitecan + pembrolizumab (ASCENT-04, approved 2026).

standardOfCare.approach: Datopotamab deruxtecan (TROPION-Breast02, OS benefit) or sacituzumab govitecan (ASCENT-03), both approved 2026; PARP inhibitor if germline BRCA; chemotherapy.
